Title: Active Learning Metamaterial Optimization Integrated Systems
Text:
Active Learning for Metamaterial Optimization on
HPC and QC Integrated Systems
Seongmin Kim
National Center for Computational Sciences
Oak Ridge National Laboratory
Oak Ridge, TN 37830, USA
Email: kims@ornl.gov
In-Saeng Suh
National Center for Computational Sciences
Oak Ridge National Laboratory
Oak Ridge, TN 37830, USA
Email: suhi@ornl.gov
Abstract—Active learning algorithms, integrating machine
learning, quantum computing and optics simulation in an itera-
tive loop, offer a promising approach to optimizing metamateri-
als. However, these algorithms can face difficulties in optimizing
highly complex structures due to computational limitations. High-
performance computing (HPC) and quantum computing (QC)
integrated systems can address these issues by enabling parallel
computing. In this study, we develop an active learning algorithm
working on HPC-QC integrated systems. We evaluate the perfor-
mance of optimization processes within active learning (i.e., train-
ing a machine learning model, problem-solving with quantum
computing, and evaluating optical properties through wave-optics
simulation) for highly complex metamaterial cases. Our results
showcase that utilizing multiple cores on the integrated system
can significantly reduce computational time, thereby enhancing
the efficiency of optimization processes. Therefore, we expect that
leveraging HPC-QC integrated systems helps effectively tackle
large-scale optimization challenges in general.
Index Terms—active learning, high-performance computing,
quantum computing, machine learning, optics simulation, meta-
material optimization
I. INTRODUCTION
Metamaterials derive their properties not only from the
inherent properties of their constituent materials but also from
their geometrical features [1]. Optimizing these geometrical
parameters is essential for achieving high performance in
practical applications. However, the complexity of their para-
metric spaces results in exceedingly large optimization spaces,
making optimization processes impractical in realistic time
frames [2]. Moreover, evaluating their properties can be time-
consuming, even with efficient physics-based approximation
or numerical methods, leading to significant computational
costs. Active learning algorithms, which iteratively combine
machine learning to generate surrogates, quantum computing
for solving the surrogates, and optical simulation to evaluate
the optical properties of the designed structure. Active learning
algorithms iteratively include informative data points, which
are predicted metamaterial structures from quantum computing
and calculated figure-of-merits(FOMs), after each optimization
cycle, improving the quality of a dataset, allowing for the
convergence toward the optimal state. These algorithms have
proven to be highly effective for optimizing metamaterials [3],
[4]. However, previous works have been limited to simple
geometries since complex structures require large volumes
of training data and extensive time to solve surrogates and
evaluate their properties [5]. In this work, to address these
challenges, we have developed an active learning algorithm
that leverages HPC-QC ecosystems [6], loosely integrated the
Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility’s (OLCF) Frontier
supercomputer (64-core AMD Optimized 3rd Gen EPYC
CPUs and 4 AMD Instinct MI250X GPUs per node) with
IBM Quantum devices through the Quantum Computing User
Program [7] (Fig. 1).
Fig. 1. The schematic of the active learning algorithm working on HPC-QC
integrated systems.
II. METHODOLOGY
A. Machine Learning
A surrogate model can be built after training a factorization
machine (FM) by describing the correlation between material
structures and their performances [8], which can be formulated
with a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO)
model. The dataset for training FM contains binary vectors
and their corresponding figure of merits (FOMs). We generate
datasets to evaluate the time required for training FM with
multi-cores on the HPC-quantum system (Frontier): the length
of a bitstring is 240, and the number of data pairs is 1,000,
3,000, 5,000, or 10,000. For example, a dataset containing


5,000 data pairs with a bitstring length of 240 is denoted as
240 x 5,000.
B. Quantum Computing
Quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) is a
promising quantum algorithm to efficiently solve QUBOs. This
algorithm iteratively optimizes its variational parameters using
both quantum and classical computers [9]. We utilize QAOA
in active learning to solve QUBO surrogates obtained after FM
training to predict a promising metamaterial structure. Here,
the problem solving time can be reduced by utilizing an HPC-
QC integrated system.
C. Wave-Optics Simulation
To calculate the performance metric (FOM) of a metama-
terial predicted by quantum computing, we utilize a transfer
matrix method (TMM), which is a highly effective tool for
evaluating optical properties [10]. However, evaluating prop-
erties of highly complex structures with numerous simulation
conditions is challenging on local computers, which can
be overcome by leveraging HPC systems. We evaluate the
performance of TMM on the Frontier for a 1,000-layered
photonic structure with numerous simulation conditions con-
sidered (from 50 to 1,000).

III. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
HPC systems are characterized by large-scale computing
infrastructures, enabling parallel computing to accelerate large
tasks. Here, a large job can be decomposed into multiple
sub-jobs, which are run on each core, reducing heavy work-
loads. We utilize the HPC system (Frontier) and implement
a message-passing interface (MPI) for parallel computing
[11]. As seen in Fig. 2A, utilizing multi-cores can accelerate
the FM training tasks, but using excessive cores can make
the training process slower due to communication overheads
between cores. Therefore, optimal FM training can be achieved
by employing 6 to 9 cores for the given datasets. In addition,
QUBO problem solving time using QAOA can be greatly
reduced on the HPC and QC integrated systems (Fig. 2B)
[12].
Fig. 3. (A) Simulation time for calculating optical properties using TMM with
different numbers of cores for different numbers of simulation conditions. (B)
Estimated time required for completing optimizations on a local computer and
Frontier.
Calculating optical properties is important to evaluate the
performance of designed metamaterials, but it often requires
significant computational efforts (extremely time-consuming).
Fig. 3A shows that using more cores greatly reduces simula-
tion time, but it converges after using 20 cores. Complex simu-
lation conditions significantly increase the total computational
time, but the Frontier handles such complexities efficiently,
enabling the optimization of complex metamaterial with a
reasonable time framework (Fig. 3B).
IV. CONCLUSION
We demonstrate the superior performance of the active
learning algorithm working on HPC-QC integrated systems
for optimizing complex metamaterials. Utilizing HPC-QC
integrated systems speeds up machine learning (∼54%) and
optics simulation tasks (∼67 times). Furthermore, it also
provides acceleration in solving given QUBO surrogates with
QAOA. We expect that this will be generalized in material
design optimization problems.
